transcript.text: Indesit dryer making a horrible squealing noise when it starts up, goes away after a few mins. Still dries fine

A squeal that is worst on start-up but fades after a few minutes, while the dryer still dries, is most often the drum-drive tension pulley (jockey/idler pulley) beginning to wear or run dry. A glazed drive belt is the next possibility. Both can quieten as they warm up. It is less typical of a serious motor fault. 1. Switch it off, unplug it and let it cool. Empty the drum and check around the drum lifters, door opening, lint filter and the filter slot for coins, hair grips, buttons or anything caught. Remove anything loose. A trapped item can squeak or rub. 2. With it still unplugged, turn the empty drum slowly by hand. Smooth and quiet points more towards a belt/pulley noise that only shows under load; a squeak, roughness or rumble by hand makes the drive or drum support more likely. 3. Avoid repeatedly running it if the squeal becomes constant, turns to grinding, the drum becomes difficult to turn, or there is a hot-rubber smell. Stop using it then, as a belt or pulley can fail and potentially cause further damage. If the drum is clear and the noise continues, it is usually an engineer repair because reaching the pulley and belt requires dismantling the dryer. It is commonly repairable, especially while it is still drying normally.
Ok, I unplugged it and checked. Nothing stuck in the door seal or filter. Turning the drum by hand it turns but feels a bit rough with a slight squeak/scrape. Model is IDC8T3B if that helps.

The roughness and slight scrape by hand make this more than just a normal start-up noise. The leading suspect is still a worn or dry jockey/idler pulley in the belt drive; it commonly squeals when cold then quietens as it warms. A worn belt is also possible. Because there is a scrape as well, the other possibility is a drum support/bearing or drum felt seal starting to wear. The pattern when you turn it by hand helps separate those: 1. Keep it unplugged and empty, then rotate the drum slowly for several full turns. - A noise or rough spot at the same point each revolution points more towards the drum support/felt area or something rubbing locally. - A more continuous squeak/roughness points more towards the idler pulley/belt drive. Avoid using it if the noise becomes constant, turns into grinding, the drum starts catching, or you smell hot rubber. The repair needs cabinet dismantling, so it is normally an engineer job rather than a safe external adjustment.
I turned it a few times and it feels like a fairly continuous rough scrape rather than one spot, but I can't say for sure. Is that enough to tell, or is there something else I should check?

It is enough to narrow it down, but not enough to identify the exact part with certainty. A fairly continuous rough scrape by hand makes a trapped object or one damaged spot less likely. The leading cause is now wear at the drum support/felt seal area; the original cold-start squeal still leaves the jockey/idler pulley or belt drive as a possible second fault. One useful final owner-safe check:
1. Keep it unplugged and empty. Open the door, hold the front inner rim of the drum and gently lift it, then let it settle. Do not force it. - Noticeable up/down movement, a clunk, or the drum sitting low points more towards worn drum support/bearing parts. - Little movement but a continuous scrape points more towards the front felt seal/support surface. Either result needs cabinet dismantling, so this is an engineer repair rather than an external adjustment. I would avoid further use if the scrape becomes loud grinding, the drum catches, or there is a hot-rubber smell. If it remains as described and is still drying, it is usually repairable, but ask the engineer to inspect the drum supports/felt seal as well as the belt and jockey pulley rather than changing only the belt.
I'm not sure how to check that properly, and with my back I can't tilt or lay the dryer down. I can't really tell if the drum lifts at the front. Is an engineer the next step then?

Yes — an engineer is the sensible next step. There is no need for you to tilt or dismantle it, particularly with your back. The cold-start squeal that fades while the dryer continues to turn and dry makes the jockey/idler tension pulley or drive belt the leading suspect. The continuous rough scrape when turning the empty drum by hand also means the engineer should inspect the drum support/felt seal and bearing/support parts, rather than simply fitting a belt. When booking, describe it as: “Indesit IDC8T3B, loud squeal on start-up which fades after a few minutes; drum feels continuously rough and lightly scrapes when turned by hand, but it still dries.” That should direct the visit towards the belt-drive and drum-support area. Until it is looked at, avoid using it if the noise becomes constant or turns to grinding, the drum starts catching, or there is a hot-rubber smell. Otherwise, this is commonly a repairable mechanical fault rather than a motor or heating fault.

candidates: Jockey/idler tension pulley starting to wear or dry (high)
Foreign object in the drum, lifter or filter area (low)
